summary: A 1970 note proposing a user-oriented protocol to connect to services by name instead of by number. It is a proposal in the early series.

eli5.summary: Instead of remembering a number, you could ask for a service by name, like using a contact's name rather than their phone number.

questions: connection by name user oriented protocol
subtitle: A proposal for a user-friendly way to connect to network services by name instead of number.

tldr.problem: Early network users found it confusing and cumbersome to connect to remote services using socket numbers and protocol details instead of simple names.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC proposes extensions to the host-to-host protocol allowing users to request connections using symbolic labels (like device names or file paths) instead of numeric socket addresses, with the local host system translating these names to socket numbers.
tldr.outcome: The proposal anticipated DNS and similar name resolution systems, though it was not widely adopted in the early network.

today: RFC 76 is an Internet Experiment document. While the specific proposal was not adopted, it anticipated many features of modern network interfaces, including domain naming systems and service discovery mechanisms that solve the same problem in today's networks.

sections.title: The Problem with Socket Numbers
sections.content:
RFC 76 addresses a usability problem at the University of Illinois Center for Advanced Computation (CAC). The center was building a network port facility for users who were unsophisticated about network communication. These users were accustomed to referring to devices and files by symbolic names in their local operating systems (like DSK for disk, LP for line printer, TECO for a text editor).

The existing protocol required users or their software to know and use socket numbers to establish connections, which was a significant barrier to adoption. The authors sought a way to present the network at the symbolic, user-friendly level rather than the low-level protocol level.
sections.eli5: Users were confused by having to remember numbers for things. They wanted to just say "line printer" like they did on their own computers.

sections.title: The Proposed Extension
sections.content:
The RFC proposes a new protocol element called RFSNL (Request for Socket Number for this Label). A user would send a request with a symbolic label (formatted as usercode/filename or device name) instead of a socket number. The destination host would respond with an acknowledgement indicating whether the resource exists, is available, or is unavailable.

The authors suggest a standard set of device labels like LP (line printer), CR (card reader), DSK (disk), and TTY (teletype terminal). More complex systems could use multi-part paths like those on the Burroughs B6500. The format supports ASCII characters and is designed to match each system's native naming conventions.
sections.eli5: You would tell the network "send me to the line printer" instead of "send me to socket 46," and the system would figure out the number and make the connection for you.

sections.title: User Session Example
sections.content:
The RFC includes a detailed example of a user session at CAC controlling processes at two remote sites (UTAH and PAOLI). The user interacts with the system at the symbolic level, entering commands like "HELLO" and specifying processes by name. Behind the scenes, the system uses the proposed protocol extensions to look up socket numbers and establish the necessary network connections.

This demonstrates how the proposed extension would integrate transparently into the user experience, hiding the complexity of socket numbers and network protocol details.
sections.eli5: The example shows how a user could type simple commands and the system would handle all the technical details of finding the right socket numbers and setting up the connections.
